name: Cinematic Brand Film (TV-Style Spot)
definition: A polished, agency-grade commercial with no one talking to camera: it opens on a striking cinematic shot (location, model or CGI product), cuts through a music-led montage of styled lifestyle, macro texture or CGI product shots (often one short feature super per shot), and closes on a logo/wordmark or offer end card.
why: Sells a premium mood and perceived brand size instead of an argument, so it lifts trust and price tolerance for aesthetic or giftable products, especially to warm-ish audiences and as a retargeting/brand layer.
how: Pick one setting/mood that matches the buyer's aspiration (rainy city, golden-hour beach, moody studio) or render the product in CGI.
Shoot 8-12 slow, well-lit shots: product hero, macro textures, hands/model using it; add one 2-4 word benefit super per shot, no voiceover.
Cut to a licensed music track and end on a clean logo + offer card.
closest_existing: Satisfying B-roll (Front-Splice) / Product Demo Ads: those buy attention or show function; this is a whole wordless TV-style brand spot selling mood and premium perception.

name: Brand Anthem Montage (Manifesto)
definition: A cinematic manifesto: opens on a bold logo or one-word line, then a fast montage of many aspirational people/moments (or one protagonist in vignettes) runs under a single VO or word-by-word super that states what the brand believes, and closes on logo + tagline.
why: Turns a commodity into an identity ('people like us use this'), building brand recall and a tribe; best for cold reach and to give the brand a point of view.
how: Write a 4-8 line belief statement about the buyer's identity, not the product (e.g. 'Your body needs it to perform, to recover, to embrace the moments').
Cut 10-15 short, high-energy lifestyle/athlete clips (stock or shot), one line of the manifesto per clip as a centered super or VO.
Show the product only in 1-2 beats, end on logo + tagline.
closest_existing: Goal / Dream Journey or Personal Story: those follow one real person's arc; this is a belief statement read over a montage of many people.

name: Cinematic Mini-Film (Brand Short Story)
definition: A 10-40s film-style micro story with a character, a setting and a small plot (a bellhop loads the bag, a man hunts the sea for his underwear, a kid's fingerprint becomes mom's necklace): the product is a prop inside the scene, there is no pitch or VO, and it ends on a title-card style logo.
why: Feels like a film scene, not an ad, so it earns attention and brand intrigue; works for fashion, gifting and lifestyle products with a strong aesthetic.
how: Write a 3-beat scene (setup, small twist/action, payoff) where the product is the object the character wants or uses.
Shoot it like cinema: one location, styled cast, slow camera, natural sound or one music cue, no talking to camera.
End on a title card with the brand name (like a film title) instead of a hard offer.
closest_existing: Scenarios / Day In The Life: those are creator-native or hypothetical; this is a scripted cinematic scene with a micro plot and a film title-card close.

name: Celebrity Spokesperson Spot
definition: A real famous person fronts the ad as the brand's spokesperson: opens on the celebrity's face/name delivering the hook to camera (selfie-style or studio), intercuts product close-ups and demo b-roll with kinetic claim supers while they keep talking, and closes back on them with a sign-off + logo/shop card.
why: The face stops the scroll and transfers trust/status instantly; works when a recognizable person (even a niche micro-celebrity or known pro) can credibly endorse the product.
how: Book the most recognizable face your niche respects (micro-celebrity, known athlete/chef/creator) and have them open with their name or a personal hook.
Intercut their lines with 4-6 hero product/demo shots, each with one bold claim super.
Close on them saying a one-line endorsement, then logo + offer card.
closest_existing: Celebrity Podcast Clip (Borrowed Authority): that borrows a real podcast clip; here the celebrity is hired and speaks directly as the brand's paid presenter.

name: Mini-Doc Portrait
definition: A cinematic 30s documentary vignette of one real, named person (athlete, mom, founder) with a name/title lower-third: they narrate their own life and routine in VO over observational footage, the product appears as part of that routine, and it closes on logo + tagline.
why: Feels like documentary truth rather than a testimonial pitch, so the claim rides on a real identity the viewer aspires to; great for supplements, fitness and performance products.
how: Find one real customer with an aspirational identity (triathlete, busy mom, fighter) and record a 2-min audio interview about their routine.
Shoot observational b-roll of their day (training, kitchen, family) with the product used naturally; add a name/title lower-third early.
Cut the best 5-6 VO lines over the footage with small captions, end on logo + tagline.
closest_existing: UGC Testimonial / Personal Story: those are selfie talk-to-camera; this is a produced observational doc with VO and a named lower-third.

name: Limited Collab Drop (IP Trailer)
definition: A hype launch for a limited-edition product co-branded with a franchise or another brand: opens on the two logos locked up ('X x Y', 'Limited Edition'), shows the co-branded pack in the franchise's world with VFX/action beats and a quick product-in-use moment, and closes on a 'limited time only / before it's gone' scarcity card.
why: Borrows a fandom's existing excitement and adds scarcity, so it pulls both fans and existing buyers into an urgent purchase; use for drops, seasonal editions and collabs.
how: Create a limited edition (collab with a creator/brand/local artist, or a seasonal theme) and design a co-branded pack.
Open on the 'X x Y Limited Edition' lockup, then 3-5 dramatic VFX/themed shots of the pack plus one quick use shot.
Close on 'Limited time only - gone when it's gone' with the shop link.
closest_existing: Reaction / Trend-Hijack (Borrowed Fame): that disguises borrowed attention as native content; this is an official co-branded product launch trailer with a scarcity close.

name: Micro Bumper (2-6s)
definition: An ultra-short 2-6s looping spot: one fixed headline or offer line sits on screen the whole time ('An icon of play. Rarely in stock.', 'the dreamiest sleepsuits for just £20') over 1-4 rapid product-in-use shots, then a logo flash; no VO, no story.
why: Costs almost nothing, loops for repeat views and hammers one message cheaply; ideal for frequency/retargeting and for testing headlines and offers fast.
how: Write one 5-8 word headline or price/offer line.
Grab 1-4 one-second clips of the product in use (or a hanger-swap of variants) and cut to 2-6s so it loops cleanly.
Keep the headline fixed on screen, add a logo flash at the end, run many headline variants.
closest_existing: Satisfying B-roll (Front-Splice): that is a scroll-stopper spliced before a longer ad; this is the whole ad in under 6s with one fixed headline.

name: Editorial Lookbook (Model Shoot Reel)
definition: A music-only, campaign-quality model shoot of the product: opens on a wide hero shot of the model in a styled location or studio, cuts between turns, back views and macro fabric/detail close-ups (often several looks or colourways), and closes on a logo or offer end card. No talking, no story, no claims.
why: For fashion, swim and jewellery the garment is the pitch: a polished shoot makes the piece look premium and aspirational in 6-20s, and it scales cheaply into one ad per SKU or drop.
how: Book one model and one strong location or seamless backdrop; shoot each piece wide, walking, turning, back view and 3-4 macro detail shots.
Cut fast to a trending or moody track (1 shot per ~1s), alternating full-body hero with fabric/detail close-ups; optionally add 'Introducing X' / 'New in' super.
End on a clean logo/offer card (e.g. '10% off everything', 'Shop the edit').
closest_existing: Try-On Haul - a haul is a creator trying on pieces on her phone and reacting; this is a brand's polished, silent editorial shoot of the product with no creator persona.

name: Fit Check (Single Outfit)
definition: Native phone-shot clip of one person in ONE complete outfit: opens mid-pose (mirror selfie, bedroom, doorway, street), then she turns, walks, twirls and shows front/back/detail to music, with a single relatable one-line caption ('dinner and drinks fit', 'never taking these off', 'what I'm wearing as a size 12'). No talking, no demo, no multiple outfits.
why: It looks exactly like an organic TikTok/IG OOTD post, so it slips past ad blindness and shows true fit and movement on a real body; perfect for one hero garment.
how: Put one creator in the full outfit (hero product + simple styling) in a real home/street spot; film handheld or propped phone, 8-15s.
Capture walk-in, slow turn, back view, hand-on-fabric detail and a confident end pose, cut to a trending sound.
Add one native-style caption line (POV / occasion / size), no logo until the end or watermark only.
closest_existing: Try-On Haul - a haul shows several pieces back to back; a fit check commits the whole ad to one outfit with no talking.

name: Styling Remix (One Piece, Many Looks)
definition: One hero item styled into several different outfits: opens with the item and a hook ('One skirt. Three lives', 'How I style my favourite boots'), cuts outfit by outfit with an occasion label each (school drop-off, lunch date, night out), and ends on 'which is your favourite?' or the product end card.
why: Sells versatility and cost-per-wear, which kills the 'where would I even wear it' objection for a single mid-priced piece.
how: Pick one hero piece and plan 3-5 outfits around it for distinct occasions.
Film same spot, same framing; open on the item in hand + hook text, then quick-cut each look with an occasion label.
Close with 'Which is your favourite?' or the product name card and offer.
closest_existing: Try-On Haul - a haul shows many different products; a remix keeps ONE product constant and changes everything around it.

name: GRWM (Get Ready With Me)
definition: Creator opens undone (robe, casual clothes, bare face) with a 'get ready / get dressed with me' hook, chats or captions through each step as she applies or puts on the product (makeup, skincare, outfit), and ends on the finished look reveal, often with a walk-out or twirl.
why: The before-to-done arc is a built-in curiosity loop that holds viewers to the reveal, and the chatty native format lets the product be used naturally instead of pitched.
how: Start the creator 'before' (robe, messy hair, no makeup) on camera with a 'GRWM for ___' text hook tied to an occasion.
Film each step of using the product in order with casual chat or captions (what it is, why she likes it); keep cuts quick.
End on the full reveal: final look, turn or walk-out, plus product/offer card.
closest_existing: UGC How-To - a how-to teaches usage step by step; GRWM is a native lifestyle ritual with chat, built around a transformation reveal and an occasion.

name: Pack My Bag (What's In My Bag)
orig: Pack My Bag (What's In My Bag)
definition: Hands (or a faceless torso) pack everyday essentials (phone, wallet, laptop, keys, lipstick, AirPods) into the bag one by one on a table or cafe bench, showing it swallows everything, then lift it onto the shoulder and close on the logo.
why: Answers the main bag/organiser objection, 'will my stuff fit?', visually and in seconds, and the satisfying packing reads as native 'what's in my bag' content.
how: Lay the bag plus 6-8 recognisable daily essentials neatly around it on a clean surface or a lifestyle spot (cafe, desk).
Film overhead or chest height as hands drop items in one at a time, showing pockets/compartments; add one line of copy ('A work bag designed for more than the office').
End with the packed bag zipped and lifted onto the shoulder, then logo.
closest_existing: Product Demo Ads - a general demo shows features in use; this is one fixed beat (packing real daily essentials) that proves capacity and organisation.

name: This or That (Pick Your Vibe)
definition: Two product variants shown side by side under a fixed header ('Choose your spooky season vibe', 'Same but different'), each labelled by name, swapping to a new pair every 1-2s for 6-8 rounds so the viewer silently picks, then ending on a full collection grid + shop CTA.
why: Turns browsing into a game: every pair is a micro-decision that keeps the viewer watching, shows the whole range fast, and makes them mentally pick a favourite before the CTA; ideal for products with many SKUs.
how: Pick 12-16 variants (colours, shapes, scents) and pair them; film each pair side by side in the same framing (e.g. two fingers, two hands, two items).
Add a fixed 'Choose your ___ vibe' header and name labels; cut a new pair every ~1.5s.
Close on a grid of the whole collection with 'Shop the collection' / offer badge, and ask 'which one are you?' in copy.
closest_existing: Ranking / Tier List - a tier list ranks options with your product on top; this lets the viewer pick between your own variants with no ranking or competitor.

name: Animated Static (Motion-Graphic Packshot)
definition: A 5-15s ad that is basically a static image ad brought to life: one product packshot (or offer card) on a designed background, a bold headline, then benefit callouts, a stat, a price/offer badge or a countdown animate in one by one, ending on the packshot + CTA. No people talking, no footage story.
why: Cheapest video asset to make and test: it gets static-ad clarity (product + promise + offer in one glance) into Reels/Stories placements, and the motion buys the extra second of attention a flat static loses.
how: Take a clean packshot (or render) of the product on a brand-colour or moody background and write one punchy headline.
Animate in 3-4 elements in sequence: benefit tags/leader-line callouts, one stat ('91% saw results'), then the offer badge or a ticking timer.
Hold on the full card for 2-3s with the CTA; export 9:16 and 4:5, swap only headline/offer for variants.
closest_existing: Text-Wall Story (Read-Along Still): both are 'one still', but that is a long first-person story to read; this is a product packshot with short callouts/offer animating in.

name: Flipbook Slideshow (Fixed Frame, Cards Flip)
definition: A 6-15s motion graphic where the frame stays locked (brand header, sale line or 'live now' label) while the image in the middle flips every ~0.5-1.5s through many cards: each product/SKU/colourway as a cutout or model+flat-lay card, or the brand's own past sale creatives. It ends on the last card or a shop-now card.
why: Shows the whole range or offer history in one scroll-stopping rhythm; the fixed headline carries the message (new drop, sale, 'we won't do this again') while the flipping cards keep eyes on it. Ideal for multi-SKU stores and sales.
how: Lock a template: brand name + one line ('Live now', 'Up to 40% off', 'We won't do this again') and a clean white or brand-colour background.
Drop in 6-12 product cutouts / colourways (or screenshots of your past sale statics), one per card, each with its name or price.
Flip a card every 0.5-1.5s to a beat, add a ticker/countdown if it's a sale, end on a shop-now card; export 9:16.
closest_existing: Try-On Haul / Collection Lookbook show range with live footage of a person; this is a pure graphic template where only the card in a fixed frame changes.

name: Offer Stack Breakdown (Here's Everything You Get)
definition: The whole ad is the deal itself: a hook that teases an unbelievable offer ('someone's getting fired', 'we need to apologize to anyone who paid full price'), then the presenter or hands pull out each item one at a time and name it ('you get X... plus Y for FREE... plus Z'), stacking value until a price/discount reveal, guarantee and 'before it's gone' close.
why: Turns a bundle or gift-with-purchase into a visible pile of value so the price feels like a steal; best for warm audiences and sale periods when you have a bundle or free gifts to push.
how: Build a bundle (main product + 2-4 cheap free add-ons) and open on an offer-shock hook like 'Don't buy X until you see this deal'.
Hold up or unpack each item one by one with a caption per item ('FREE glass bottle', 'PLUS a travel bag'), keeping a running 'and you also get...' rhythm.
Reveal total value vs price (or % off / per-unit price), add the guarantee, and close with urgency ('grab it before it's gone').
closest_existing: Unboxing (First-Open Reveal) - unboxing is about the first-impression reveal of one product; here every beat is a priced offer item and the ad is built around the deal math, not the product experience.

name: Video Static (Caption Over Looping B-roll)
definition: A 5-20s ad that is basically a static ad that moves: one silent, lo-fi b-roll loop of the product (pour, stir, fizz, held bottle) with a single headline or meme caption burned on top (sometimes a few benefit tags or a short rolling caption list), no voiceover or presenter, ending on the same shot or a quick product/offer card.
why: As cheap as a static image to make but plays as native video, so you can test dozens of headlines/angles fast; best for consumables and any product with a satisfying visual action.
how: Film one 5-10s phone clip of the product's best action (pour, mix, open, spray, wear) in natural light.
Burn one strong headline on top (question, POV, 'X for less than $Y', relatable line) plus 2-4 small benefit/price tags if needed.
Export 3-10 versions with different headlines on the same loop and let spend pick the winner.
closest_existing: Text-Wall Story (Read-Along Still) - that is one still image carrying a long story; here it is a moving product loop with a single short headline, no story and no dwell-time read.

name: AI Story VSL (Cinematic Caption Story)
definition: A 45-120s story-VSL told entirely through AI-generated, film-look scenes with burned-in captions (often with VO): it opens on a humiliating or emotional moment from the buyer's or spouse's point of view ('At 43 I had to ask for an XXL', 'My wife came home and froze'), shows the struggle and failed fixes, reveals the hidden cause with a 3D mechanism shot, then the product, the transformation scenes and a guarantee/offer close. No real presenter carries the ad.
why: Gets the emotional pull of a long advertorial story with cinematic visuals you could never afford to shoot; best for problem-aware supplements and health/wellness products with a 'hidden cause' angle.
how: Write a 60-90s first-person (or spouse's) story script: embarrassing moment -> 'I was doing everything right' -> real hidden cause -> product -> life after -> guarantee.
Generate one consistent AI character across 10-15 cinematic scenes plus 1-2 3D mechanism shots (organ/cell glow), and burn each script line on as a caption.
Close on real product-in-hand footage and the offer (guarantee, bundle, 'link below').
closest_existing: Personal Story [TOF,MOF] - same story arc, but here no creator is on camera: the whole story is acted out in AI cinematic scenes with captions/VO, plus a built-in mechanism reveal like a VSL.

name: Meme Caption Loop (Relatable Joke Clip)
definition: A 4-10s single-shot (or quick-montage) clip with one relatable meme-format caption ('Me cancelling my $900 dental surgery after...', 'When you know who the killer is but can't prove it yet', 'Forever girl who needs something in her arms to fall asleep'), no voiceover, product visible in frame; it ends when the loop ends.
why: Reads as a meme post rather than an ad, so it gets shared and watched to the end; same build as Video Static, only the caption is a relatable joke instead of a product headline.
how: Film or source a 5-8s clip of someone (or a pet) using the product in a funny or relatable moment.
Write one 'Me when...' / 'When you...' caption that ties the joke to the product's benefit.
Burn it on in native TikTok/IG text style, no VO, and test several captions on the same clip.
closest_existing: Reaction / Trend-Hijack (Borrowed Fame) - that borrows an existing viral clip or trend; here it is the brand's own simple clip with a meme caption. Structurally identical to Video Static, so merged as its meme-caption variant.

name: Meme Montage (Chaos Edit)
definition: A voiceover (or punchy one-word captions) carries the pitch while the picture cuts every 1-2s to a different borrowed or absurd clip - archival B&W film, movie/anime moments, stunts, stock disasters, glitch zooms, cut-out meme stickers - with big word-by-word captions; the product only appears in a beat or two near the end, then a logo/CTA.
why: The 'brainrot' edit pace makes it impossible to scroll past and lets a dry message (mechanism, comfort, ingredients) feel like entertainment; best for younger, meme-literate audiences and brands with a playful voice.
how: Write a tight 20-45s VO or caption script for the product's one key claim (problem -> mechanism -> product).
Cut a visual every 1-2s that literally or absurdly illustrates each word (archival clips, movie/anime moments, stock disasters, stunts), with glitch/zoom transitions and bold word-by-word captions.
Land the product in the last 5-8s (founder or hand holding it) and end on logo + one-line CTA.
closest_existing: Reaction / Trend-Hijack (Borrowed Fame) - that borrows one existing viral clip or trend and reacts to it; here dozens of unrelated borrowed/absurd clips are spliced under your own VO as pure edit style.

name: Multi-Panel Split Screen
definition: The vertical frame is cut into 2-9 panels that all play at the same time for the whole ad: e.g. on-model 360 spin, macro fabric/detail loop, back view, several body types or several outfits, with a small brand/product label or one title tile ('Fall '26 is here', 'Stretchy jeans will change your life'); no VO or presenter, 6-15s.
why: Shows fit, detail, movement and range in one glance with no edit for the eye to wait on, so it works as a richer catalog ad; best for apparel, underwear and anything where fit plus texture sells.
how: Shoot 3-4 short clips of the same product: on-model spin, back view, close-up texture/detail, and a second model or colourway.
Stack them as 3-4 horizontal panels (or a 3x3 grid for a collection) all looping at once, aligned to the same beat.
Add the brand + product name (or one headline tile) and keep it 6-15s with no VO.
closest_existing: Try-On Haul [MOF] - a haul shows one creator trying pieces one after another with talking; here several silent views play at the same time in split panels, like a moving catalog page.

name: Not For Everyone (Reverse Qualifier)
definition: Opens with reverse psychology - 'Don't buy X', '3 reasons you SHOULDN'T buy X', 'Honestly, this isn't for everyone' - then runs a list of sarcastic or tongue-in-cheek disqualifiers ('if you're okay with blades that dull in months', 'if the pharmacy creams are working', 'you're just not that into glowing skin (said no one ever)'), each one secretly a benefit, before flipping to 'but if you want...' and closing on proof plus a guarantee/CTA.
why: The 'don't buy' hook breaks ad blindness and makes the viewer qualify themselves in, so the pitch feels like honest filtering rather than selling; great for premium-priced products and markets tired of hype.
how: Open on a 'Don't buy [product] if...' / 'This isn't for everyone' line on the hero shot or a creator to camera.
List 3-5 disqualifiers that are really the pains your product solves (shown as captions, sticky notes or product demo shots, each with a wink).
Flip to 'But if you want [result]...', show one proof point or mechanism, and close on the guarantee and CTA.
closest_existing: Myth Buster [TOF,MOF] - myth buster corrects a false belief; here the whole ad is framed as reasons NOT to buy, and each 'reason' is a disguised benefit before the flip.

name: Review Read-Aloud (Owner Reads Real Reviews)
definition: The owner, founder or an expert host sits with a tablet/laptop (selfie or podcast set) and goes through real customer reviews or customer-submitted before/after photos one at a time, each shown on screen as a screenshot/photo card, reading them aloud and reacting/explaining; often opens by addressing a skeptic ('these positive reviews are all bought!') and closes with the guarantee and link. Usually long (1-5 min).
why: Turns a pile of reviews into a personal, believable walkthrough that answers 'are these real?' head-on; best for warm/retargeting audiences and products with lots of strong written reviews or customer photos.
how: Open on the objection: read a skeptical comment ('your reviews are fake') or tease 'let's look at what you sent us'.
Sit with a tablet and read 5-10 real reviews (or react to before/after photos) one by one, overlaying each as a Trustpilot/review screenshot and adding a short comment on each.
Close by restating the guarantee ('if it doesn't work you get your money back') and pointing to the link.
closest_existing: UGC Testimonial Mashup [BOF] - that cuts together clips of customers speaking; here no customer appears, the owner/host reads their written reviews or photos aloud and reacts to each.

Open on the finished result, then shoot hands/creator assembling it step by step with a clear branded pack shot as the product goes in.

definition: The whole ad is one transformation: opens on the 'before' (shaggy hair in the barber chair, frizzy curls, a 'Day 0' body/face), the middle shows the product doing the work (a pro cutting and styling with it, or an AI morph sliding from Day 0 to Day 90), and it closes on the big 'after' reveal plus product card/offer.

how: Pick the most dramatic 'before' you can show (real client in the chair, or an AI-generated Day 0 image) with a hook caption like 'every transformation…' or 'Face fat? gone'.
Show the product in action mid-ad: pro applying/styling it, or a smooth morph with the product pack sitting in frame.
Hold on the 'after' (turn, hair flip, Day 90 label), then cut to a clean product shot with price/offer.

definition: An expert in a white coat (or just hands) explains how the problem works using an everyday object as a stand-in for the body: opens on the prop and a hook ('nobody wants to be the short kid', 'double cleansing: scam?'), the middle acts the mechanism out on the prop (orange peel = pores, tube = urethra, pool noodle = growth plate, straw = blood vessel), and it closes with the product as the fix plus offer.

Script 30-60s where every claim is shown on the prop: the problem happening, why common fixes fail, what your product's ingredient does.

definition: A relatable person states a problem and the confusion ('hundreds of products... which one do I even need?'), says an expert built a short quiz, then a screen recording walks through the quiz questions and the 'calculating your results' screen, closing on 'take the free 2-minute quiz, link below'.
why: Sells a free personalised answer instead of a product, lowering friction for cold traffic and segmenting buyers into the right SKU.
how: Build a 4-6 question quiz that routes to your product/bundle (Typeform, Octane AI, Shopify quiz app).
Film a person with the problem + 'which one do I need?' confusion, then screen-record answering the quiz.
End on the results-loading screen and a 'take the free quiz' CTA.
closest_existing: Q&A - there the creator answers a question; here the call-to-action is the quiz itself and the ad demos taking it.

name: BTS vs Final Shot Reveal
definition: Opens on the raw behind-the-scenes setup (rig, tripod, suction mount, studio) capturing a shot, then cuts to the polished final footage it produced, alternating setup vs result a few times and ending on the brand card.
why: Proves the product's output quality directly - the viewer sees exactly what they'd get - ideal for tools that produce a result (camera gear, lighting, editing, beauty tools).
how: Film the product set up doing its job in a plain/messy real environment (the 'how').
Capture or render the clean final result it produces (the 'wow').
Cut setup > result 2-4 times with a 'POV: no crew, just this' caption, end on product + offer.
closest_existing: Product Demo Ads - a demo shows use; this hinges on the contrast reveal between the scrappy setup and the polished output it created.

name: Campaign Shoot Vlog (On Set BTS)
orig: BTS vs Final Shot Reveal (split out: 1517291476835118, 2304623477006623)
definition: Lo-fi phone vlog from the brand's own campaign/photo shoot: opens 'we're on set for our ... shoot', then handheld clips of models/founder changing, crew, lights, mood boards and between-take moments showing the new collection, closing on a final look or group shot.
why: Shows a new collection on real bodies in an exciting insider context, so it reads as native content rather than a polished catalogue ad.
how: During any product photoshoot, have someone film vertical handheld BTS: setup, outfit changes, models laughing, shot review.
Add casual narrator captions ('we're on set for...', 'she wants to frame this one').
Cut 30-60s, end on the best final look or a lineup of the pieces.

name: Torture Test (Try To Break It)
definition: The whole ad is a sequence of escalating abuse or stress attempts on the product (flips, jumps, drops, water, weight) with it surviving each one, ending on the verdict shot ('still in / still works') and brand.
why: Visual proof of durability or fit beats any claim and the escalation keeps people watching to see if it finally fails.
how: List 5-7 increasingly extreme tests relevant to your product's promise (falls out? breaks? leaks?).
Film each in one clean shot with a short caption, hardest test last.
End on the intact product + a 'still going' verdict and offer.
closest_existing: Product Demo Ads / Challenge - a demo shows normal use; this is a pure escalating stress test where survival is the payoff.

name: YouTube Reviewer Clip (Borrowed Expert)
definition: A horizontal, letterboxed excerpt from an independent long-form YouTube reviewer: often opens on a YouTube-style thumbnail hook, then the reviewer talks through and handles the product with screen recordings/specs, with a branded header bar, closing on 'see full review on YouTube' or a shop end card.
why: An independent niche expert's real review carries authority no brand claim has; the YouTube look signals unsponsored, in-depth content.
how: Send product to niche YouTubers and license a 30-80s segment of their review.
Keep it horizontal with black bars, add a product-name header and burned-in captions; optional thumbnail-style opener.
Close with end card or 'full review on YouTube + discount code'.
closest_existing: Celebrity Podcast Clip / UGC Reviews - this borrows a niche YouTube reviewer's long-form review (letterboxed), not a famous podcast or a vertical UGC creator.

name: Trade-Show Booth Demo
definition: Founder/rep with a lanyard filmed at an expo booth (banners, crowd) pitching and demoing the product live to camera, intercut with bold spec cards and a 'NEW' badge, closing on the rep summing up and the brand card.
why: The expo setting signals a real, industry-recognised launch and makes a pitch feel like news coverage rather than an ad.
how: Film at a trade show, pop-up or market stall with branded backdrop - rep demos the product live.
Intercut 3-4 full-screen spec cards (key numbers) between demo shots, add a 'NEW' sticker.
End with the rep's one-line summary to camera + logo card.
closest_existing: Stage Talk / Keynote Authority - no stage or audience lecture; it is a hands-on booth demo with spec cards, closer to a news segment from the show floor.

name: Good-Deed Vlog (Giving It Away)
definition: The brand owner vlogs explaining the product in the shop, then delivers/donates it to a community hero group (e.g. a police K9 unit), filming the handover, the recipients' thank-yous and why it matters, ending on the brand card.
why: Goodwill and a respected recipient make the brand likeable and quietly endorse the product's usefulness.
how: Pick a sympathetic recipient that genuinely needs the product (rescue shelter, nurses, K9 unit, coaches).
Film the owner explaining the product, then the real handover and reactions in one continuous vlog.
Close with the recipients' thanks and a soft brand/offer card.
closest_existing: Gift Reaction Reveal - that focuses on one person's emotional unwrap; this is an owner vlog of a donation to a community group, with the product explained along the way.
